Bottom line: no other paper on ICCAD 2026 Problem A is public on arXiv yet. I also scanned every arXiv abstract containing 'netlist' posted from 2026-07 onward (47 papers) and 'EDA agent tool' from 2026-06 onward, and none is a same-benchmark paper. The concurrent work is real, though, as a DAC manuscript plus several public code releases and artifacts:

(1) DIRECT CONCURRENT PAPER. Zhangjin Zhao (SUSTech), team cada1078, Honorable Mention, 661.4/674. Their homepage lists 'Verifiable LLM Agent Framework for EDA (gate-level netlist case study)' as 'Manuscript under review at DAC'. The mechanism is close to our C1: schema-typed tool calls, a persistent design state, and propose-verify-commit (snapshot → Yosys/ABC CEC + structural checks → commit or rollback). It could be the 'Beyond Equivalence' paper, but I could not confirm that. Recommendation: assume a same-benchmark DAC 2027 competitor. Our differentiators are:
- the routing-only closed catalog with live-state grounding, one retry and safe no-op;
- the register-cut proposition (A1-A4);
- the equivalence-vs-conformance 'drift' separation;
- C2 (catalog vs bare list vs BM25 vs supervised classifiers);
- C3 (fault injection);
- a higher final score (671.366 vs 661.4).

The full combination was not found on arXiv in this angle: an LLM that only selects one intent from a closed catalog of deterministic netlist operations, with name params grounded against the current mutated state and one retry then a no-op, plus a register-cut CEC proof before commit with rollback, plus an explicit split between the functional guarantee and request conformance, with drift persisting across later requests. Answers to the three key questions:

(a) Does catalog/description content dominate? Yes, this direction is well established:
- Hsieh et al. 2023: docs alone match or beat demonstrations.
- Intent-description work: Parikh 2023 (ACL Industry), Hong 2024 (SIGDIAL), Hu et al. 2024 (2407.17862; +11.24 for descriptions over tokenized labels, encoder-based).
- Description text drives selection: Faghih 2025 (EMNLP; over 10x usage from edited descriptions), BiasBusters (2510.00307, ICLR 2026).
- Description engineering: MCP-smells 2602.14878 (+5.85 pp), Trace-Free+ 2602.20426, JTPRO 2604.19821 (ACL 2026 Findings), DocsChisel 2608.10037, EASYTOOL, PLAY2PROMPT.
- Most directly, Kulkarni (NeurIPS 2026 WiML) tests 'contrastive boundary descriptions' against similar-tool confusion, which is essentially our 'disambiguation' section. Cite it as concurrent.
- Our 61.4% to 88.4% jump is much larger than the gains in the MCP-smells work, which is worth stating.

(b) Example-request retrieval vs doc retrieval:
- Prior work mostly retrieves tool docs (RAG-MCP, ToolRet, Tool-DE 2510.22670, Re-Invoke) or retrieves demonstrations when docs are weak (Xu 2023: up to +90%; TinyAgent; SEER 2508.15214; BAR 2508.14323).
- Tool2Vec (2409.02141) argues that query-based tool representations beat description-based ones for retrieval.
- For intents, Milios 2023, Arora 2024, APEX (2611.09491, Nov 2026) and Dynamic Label Name Refinement (2412.15603) use retrieved labeled examples.
- I found no paper measuring example retrieval layered on a full in-prompt catalog and showing it adds about +1 pt. This looks like our most distinctive data point. It is consistent with Hsieh 2023 and Baek 2025, where long-context example selection is about as good as random.
- Scope the claim: retrieval-helps results (RAG-MCP, Less-is-More DATE 2025, LongFuncEval 2505.10570, ToolChoiceConfusion 2606.06284) involve much larger catalogs or tool retrieval rather than example retrieval.

(c) Near-synonym confusion as the main residual error: already documented. Sources include MetaTool's similar-choice subtask, Rabinovich and Anaby-Tavor (8-19% drops from semantically related tools vs smaller paraphrase drops), AutoTools Table 7 (44% of errors are selection errors that confuse similar tools), DiaFORGE, ToolScope, Kulkarni, and NTILC 2606.06566. An MDPI Algorithms paper, 'Too Many Tools, Too Much Confusion?' (doi 10.3390/a19060447), names 'retrieval collisions among semantically similar tools' as a dominant failure. I saw only snippets of it because the page returned 403. Present (c) as a confirming observation.

Short answer: the idea "AI-produced circuit change is kept only after an equivalence proof, otherwise rejected or rolled back" is NOT new, so the paper should not claim that guard as a contribution. It is already published in three places:
(a) Offline LLM evolution of EDA or verification tool code. Self-Evolved ABC (DAC'26) is the closest. It runs ABC cec/dsat after every code change, checks sequential designs with a depth-1 BMC (combinational logic feeding each register, essentially our register cut), rejects on any mismatch and rolls back on QoR regression. Similar: MappingEvolve (DAC'26, CEC as a reward penalty), IC3-Evolve (IJCAI'26, certificate-gated) and SATLUTION (DRAT-gated).
(b) LLM RTL optimization or generation with an equivalence filter. RTLRewriter (ICCAD'24) keeps a rewrite only if it passes equivalence checking and improves QoR. Also SymRTLO (NeurIPS'25), ASPEN (MLCAD'25: Z3-proved rewrite rules plus a final commercial LEC) and FormalRTL (2026: accept only on C-RTL equivalence proof).
(c) Correct-by-construction generation: Circuit Transformer (ICLR'25).

What we did NOT find in any paper:
1. A closed-catalog router where the LLM never writes netlists or code, evaluated on a paraphrase stress set.
2. Per-request transactional commit over ONE persistent, already-mutated netlist, with names grounded against the current state.
3. A stated soundness proposition with explicit assumptions (complete mediation, sound checker, faithful projection, correct structural checks).
4. An explicit split between the functional guarantee and request conformance ("drift"), backed by fault injection.
Two recent surveys support this. arXiv 2610.10580 (Oct 2026) calls LLM+LEC "relatively immature" and lists only DeepRTL2, FormalEval and FormalRTL. arXiv 2512.23189 cites no equivalence-gated agent edits and no gate-level ECO agents. Closest conceptual neighbours for the guarantee-vs-conformance framing:
- "Beyond Equivalence: Task-Level Verification..." (NeurIPS'26, Arnold et al.) argues equivalence is too STRONG a contract. Its title nearly collides with the concurrent paper we already cite, so double-check that bib entry.
- IRONPROOF (2610.11073) states that its proof only holds relative to its own intermediate representation, which is analogous to our assumption A3.

CRITICAL concurrent same-contest work: Zhangjin Zhao et al. (team cada1078, Honorable Mention, 661.4/674). Their homepage says a DAC manuscript is "under review". It describes schema-typed tool calls, a deterministic layer over a persistent design state, and propose-verify-commit on a snapshot with CEC (Yosys/ABC SAT miter) plus structural-constraint checks and rollback. That is a direct overlap with the C1 mechanism, possibly in the same DAC cycle. From the public text, the differences are: their LLM is a planner, not a one-intent closed-catalog router; no stated proposition; no paraphrase routing study; no fault injection.
A second public same-contest artifact also overlaps: github.com/JerryFlyTiger/netlist-agent (LLM picks one of 65 typed schemas, every transform ABC-CEC-checked).
A contest blog (ynl.it.com) describes pre-validation of hallucinated signal and gate names, which overlaps our grounding step.
Suggested framing: claim the empirical routing study (C2), the closed-catalog plus current-state grounding design, the formal proposition with its assumptions, and the drift and fault-injection results (C3) as contributions. Present CEC-gated commit and rollback as an established pattern and cite Self-Evolved ABC and RTLRewriter for it.

It is a fork of CAD-Contest-2026-ProblemA/Agent, and its README describes the exact system: one {intent, params} object, BM25 over labelled requests, register-cut ABC CEC with rollback. It is public, search-indexed and named "Fail-Closed", so a search for "fail-closed LLM netlist agent" surfaces it. all_papers.title: Verifiable LLM Agent Framework for EDA (gate-level netlist case study) [unpublished manuscript, under review at DAC; ICCAD 2026 CAD Contest Problem A, team cada1078, Honorable Mention]
all_papers.authors: Zhangjin Zhao (first author; SUSTech) et al.
all_papers.venue: Manuscript under review at DAC (per author homepage); not found on arXiv
all_papers.what_it_does: This is another team in the same ICCAD 2026 Problem A contest. Their LLM (GPT-4o-mini or Claude Haiku 4.5) works as a semantic parser and planner that emits schema-typed tool calls: 81 JSON-schema tools built from relational operators over netlist relations, via native function calling. A deterministic executor applies every edit under propose-verify-commit: the edit runs on a snapshot, is checked by combinational equivalence (Yosys/ABC SAT miter) plus structural-constraint checks, and is then committed or rolled back. They report 661.4/674 on the hidden set.
all_papers.overlap_note: This is the closest work found. It hits C1 almost one-to-one: same contest and setting, an LLM limited to a closed typed catalog (81 tools against our ~80), snapshot, equivalence check, then commit or rollback. It appears to be under review at DAC too, so it is concurrent and double-blind. Its public description shows none of the following: grounding against the live state with one retry and a safe no-op, register-cut DFF pseudo-I/O, the A1-A4 proposition, the split between equivalence and request conformance (drift), the routing ablations (C2) or fault injection (C3). Those are the differentiators to stress. Our 671.4 is above their 661.4/674.

all_papers.title: AgenticECO: An Agentic Framework for ECO on 3D Integrated Circuits
all_papers.authors: Shuo Ren, Yaohui Han, Libo Shen, et al. (incl. Bei Yu, Tsung-Yi Ho)
all_papers.what_it_does: An 'evidence-gated tool-using agent workflow' for post-route ECO with a fixed set of 7 typed operations (eco_route, move_cells, full_reroute, gui_render, drc/sta/power) and no free-form Tcl. The orchestrator synthesizes a deterministic repair program whose candidates are registered before execution. An independent verifier that 'consumes no model text' checks routing, DRC, max/min timing, structural equivalence (explicitly 'no formal LEC') and byte-identical preservation of untouched nets. 'A pass commits X′, whereas a fail rolls back to X' (copy-on-write). It calls this a 'fail-closed verification boundary'.
all_papers.overlap_note: C1: same fail-closed commit/rollback pattern, closed typed operation set and model-independent verifier in an EDA agent, and it already uses the phrase 'fail-closed'. Differences: physical ECO rather than NL requests on a netlist; no routing of free-form requests; equivalence is structural, not a formal CEC proof; the LLM writes a repair program; no stated soundness proposition. Must cite and contrast.

all_papers.title: LATCH: LLM-Assisted Timing Closure Harness for Post-Route FPGA Optimisation
all_papers.authors: Shu Gu, Matthew Youngman, Yuqin Zhao, et al.

With expert-written recipes (the LLM returns ranked recipe IDs), functional success is 98.2%. With allow-listed Tcl operations it is in between, and with LLM-constructed procedures it falls to 17.9%. A candidate that fails checks (checkpoint reopens, routing complete, Fmax, and functional simulation of 5x200 vectors against the start design) or regresses 'reverts to its parent checkpoint'.
all_papers.overlap_note: C1 and C2, concurrent (about 4 weeks old). Same thesis that a closed catalog of predefined operations beats LLM-constructed procedures, plus verify-then-revert. Differences: FPGA timing closure, no NL request stream, functional check is random simulation rather than a formal equivalence proof, no grounding or no-op path, frontier models rather than frozen mini models.

all_papers.title: Natural Language Interface for Firewall Configuration
all_papers.authors: F. Taghiyev, A. Aslanbayli

Its validation is policy/syntax/referential, not an equivalence proof over persistent mutated state, and it has no functional-vs-intent split.

all_papers.title: CogEEGAgent: Toward Autonomous Cognitive EEG Analysis with Grounded Execution and Selection-Aware Verification
all_papers.authors: Dengzhe Hou, Lingyu Jiang, Fangzhou Lin et al.
all_papers.what_it_does: The LLM maps NL analysis questions onto registered MNE-Python analyses. Deterministic components validate typed contracts, gate confirmation and authorize evidence-bound release, and preflight validation blocks unwanted analyses (fail-closed). It separates 'semantic from scientific authority'.
all_papers.overlap_note: Same architectural idea as C1 in another domain: a closed set of registered operations, typed-contract validation, fail-closed, the LLM only interprets intent. It is read-only analysis with no mutation/commit/equivalence gate.

all_papers.title: A Methodology for Selecting and Composing Runtime Architecture Patterns for Production LLM Agents
all_papers.authors: Vasundra Srinivasan
all_papers.what_it_does: Names the 'stochastic-deterministic boundary' (SDB): a four-part contract among a proposer (LLM), a verifier, a commit step and a reject signal that governs how LLM output becomes a system action. It catalogs six runtime patterns.
all_papers.overlap_note: The generic proposer/verifier/commit/reject vocabulary matches C1's fail-closed pipeline exactly. It shows the pattern is being codified as general architecture, so C1's novelty must be the EDA instantiation (sound CEC gate, grounding, soundness proposition), not the pattern itself.

all_papers.title: Cordon: Semantic Transactions for Tool-Using LLM Agents
all_papers.authors: Zheng Chen, Hanqing Liu, Duling Xu et al.
all_papers.what_it_does: A transactional runtime that binds tool intents to reversible shadow state and an effect outbox. It validates composed execution before it commits state or releases external effects, which gives task-scoped commit/rollback/recovery/audit.
all_papers.overlap_note: Prior and concurrent art for C1's 'mutate on snapshot, commit only after check, else rollback'. It is generic systems work and its checks are not formal functional-equivalence proofs.

all_papers.title: Don't Let the Model Write the YAML: Deterministic, Minimal-Diff GitOps Remediation from LLM-Proposed Field Changes
all_papers.authors: Pruthvi Davineni
all_papers.what_it_does: Shows that LLM-authored diffs and full-file rewrites of Kubernetes manifests silently misapply (about 14-20%) or drop fields non-deterministically. Proposes that the agent emit only a structured (resource, field, value) intent, applied by a deterministic span-replacing pipeline. Whether the change is right is left to human PR review.
all_papers.overlap_note: Strong supporting analog for C1's 'the LLM never writes the artifact'. It has empirical evidence that model-written edits corrupt state. It has no formal check before commit and no closed op catalog beyond field-set.
all_papers.verified_by: abs page fetched (two fetches, including the failure-rate numbers)

all_papers.title: Less Is More: Measuring How LLM Involvement affects Chatbot Accuracy in Static Analysis
all_papers.authors: Krishna Narasimhan
all_papers.what_it_does: Compares three architectures for NL static-analysis queries: direct query generation, a schema-constrained JSON IR with deterministic query construction, and tool-augmented agentic generation. The typed IR wins by 15-25 pts over direct generation and beats the agentic approach at lower cost.
all_papers.overlap_note: Directly supports the 'Routing, Not Reasoning' thesis (C1/C2): constraining the LLM to a typed IR plus deterministic code beats letting it reason or write. Different domain, and no formal commit gate.

all_papers.title: When JSON Is Not Enough: Semantic Reliability of Schema-Constrained LLM Ordering Agents
all_papers.authors: Yin Li
all_papers.what_it_does: OrderBench: LLMs act as 'transaction compilers' that emit structured objects for an API. Over 2,400 calls, it shows 100% schema validity yet only about 80% semantic success, plus unsafe acceptances. It concludes that structured output is 'not a substitute for domain verification and fail-closed execution'.
all_papers.overlap_note: Empirical support for C1's functional-vs-conformance split and for 'drift': schema- or check-valid output can still be the wrong intent. Cite when motivating why the equivalence guarantee is not a request-conformance guarantee.

all_papers.title: LEANGUARD: Lean-Verified Guardrails for Tool-Using Agents
all_papers.authors: Sreehari Sankar, Debargha Ganguly, Vikash Singh et al.
all_papers.what_it_does: A runtime that checks every proposed tool call against a Lean4 policy (state predicates plus past-time temporal operators) before it reaches the environment. Evaluation is fail-closed, and the decision procedure is proved equivalent to a LeanLTL semantics. Feedback- or proof-guided repair handles violations.
all_papers.overlap_note: Concurrent (one week old) fail-closed, formally grounded pre-execution gating of agent actions. It addresses C1's general mechanism, but it checks policy compliance of calls, not functional equivalence of artifact transformations.

all_papers.title: Symbolic Temporal Supervision of LLM Agents Using Contracts
all_papers.authors: Yifeng Xiao, Pierluigi Nuzzo
all_papers.what_it_does: ContrAgent formalizes agent behavior as traces of tool calls over fixed checkable predicates. Assume-guarantee LTLf contracts compile to DFAs that gate actions before execution (blocking violations) and audit traces offline.
all_papers.overlap_note: Contract-checked tool calls with deterministic verdicts, related to C1's guards and the A1-A4 assumption framing. Nuzzo is well known in the EDA/formal community, so DAC reviewers may know it. It checks temporal safety policies, not equivalence.

all_papers.title: GoEX: Perspectives and Designs Towards a Runtime for Autonomous LLM Applications
all_papers.authors: Shishir G. Patil, Tianjun Zhang, Vivian Fang et al.
all_papers.what_it_does: Proposes 'post-facto validation' of LLM actions, supported by an undo capability and damage confinement. The GoEX runtime implements these for REST/DB/filesystem actions.
all_papers.overlap_note: Early prior art for undo/rollback and confinement of LLM-generated actions (C1's snapshot + rollback). We already cite Gorilla, and GoEX is the same group's execution-safety work, so cite it explicitly.

all_papers.title: Large Language Models for Structured Clinical Data Analysis: Dual-Agent Grounding and Validation (CLEAR-Med)
all_papers.authors: Erfan D. Dehkalani, Seetha Shankaran, Abbot R. Laptook et al.
all_papers.what_it_does: An NL->SQL agent plus deterministic checks and a separate cross-provider validation agent. These accept the draft, request one bounded repair, or abstain, and unresolved cases fail closed. Numerical claims stay linked to the executed SQL.
all_papers.overlap_note: Mirrors C1's 'one corrective retry, then safe no-op' policy in NL-to-SQL. Unlike ours, the LLM writes SQL and validation is partly LLM-based.

all_papers.title: IaC-Guard-V: A Verification Framework for LLM-Generated Infrastructure-as-Code Repairs
all_papers.authors: Lokesh Chauhan
all_papers.what_it_does: Verifies LLM Terraform/Kubernetes repairs along four separate axes: syntactic validity, target-issue resolution, regression safety and patch minimality. Benchmark of 70 artifacts and 630 runs.
all_papers.overlap_note: Explicitly separates 'no regressions' (our equivalence guarantee) from 'the intended fix was achieved' (our request conformance) in an IaC setting, which is relevant to C1's guarantee split. It is an evaluation framework rather than a commit gate.

all_papers.title: Evaluating LLM-driven User-Intent Formalization for Verification-Aware Languages
all_papers.authors: Shuvendu K. Lahiri
all_papers.what_it_does: Argues that checking code against a spec is mechanical, but there is 'no algorithmic way' to ensure the spec matches informal user intent. Proposes symbolic testing of specs to evaluate LLM-generated Dafny specs.
all_papers.overlap_note: The canonical formal-methods statement of the gap C1 makes explicit: a sound check gives functional correctness, not intent conformance. Cite as the conceptual anchor for the functional-vs-drift split. FMCAD readers overlap with DAC.

all_papers.title: VeriSafe Agent: Safeguarding Mobile GUI Agent via Logic-based Action Verification
all_papers.authors: Jungjae Lee, Dongjae Lee, Chihun Choi et al.
all_papers.what_it_does: Autoformalizes the user's NL instruction into a logic spec and verifies each mobile-GUI action against it at runtime, before the action takes effect (94-98% verification accuracy).
all_papers.overlap_note: Takes the opposite design choice to ours: it tries to verify intent conformance by formalizing intent, where we verify only functional preservation and measure drift. Reviewers may ask 'why not check intent?', so cite to position C1's split.

all_papers.title: From Intents to Algorithms: Verified Algorithm Discovery for Transport Networks (VERA-TN)
all_papers.authors: Behnam Ojaghi, Ricard Vilalta, Raul Muñoz
all_papers.what_it_does: In intent-based networking, the LLM only varies typed request-ordering and path-ranking programs. A trusted allocator separately enforces path validity, latency and capacity. The authors prove feasibility preservation 'under explicit assumptions'.
all_papers.overlap_note: An IBN analog of C1: an untrusted LLM in a typed sandbox, a trusted deterministic core, and a safety proposition under explicit assumptions (like our A1-A4).

all_papers.title: Graph-Symbolic Policy Enforcement and Control (G-SPEC): A Neuro-Symbolic Framework for Safe Agentic AI in 5G Autonomous Networks
all_papers.authors: Divya Vijay, Vignesh Ethiraj
all_papers.what_it_does: LLM agent plans for 5G core remediation are validated by a Network Knowledge Graph plus SHACL constraints before execution. Zero safety violations and 94.1% remediation success on a simulated 450-node core.
all_papers.overlap_note: An intent-based-networking analog of LLM proposes, symbolic validator gates execution (C1). It uses policy/constraint validation rather than an equivalence proof, and there is no closed operation catalog.

all_papers.title: What do LLMs need to Synthesize Correct Router Configurations? (Verified Prompt Programming)
all_papers.authors: Rajdeep Mondal, Alan Tang, Ryan Beckett et al.
all_papers.what_it_does: GPT-4 drafts router configurations, and verifiers (formal specs plus error localization) feed targeted corrections back. This is 'Verified Prompt Programming' for Cisco->Juniper translation and no-transit policies, with a human still in the loop.
all_papers.overlap_note: Foundational generate-then-verify for network configs, a strong analog for 'formal check before deploy'. Here the LLM writes the configs, which C1 avoids.

all_papers.title: Verified Learning for Compiler Optimization: An LLM-Guided Architecture with Formal Control
all_papers.authors: Dev Pratap Singh, Rong Feng, Suman Saha
all_papers.what_it_does: A fine-tuned code LLM proposes LLVM-IR rewrites (lazification). Alive2 formally checks semantic preservation, invalid rewrites are regenerated, and no semantic violations were observed in accepted output.
all_papers.overlap_note: An equivalence-gated LLM transformation (the C1 commit gate) in compilers. The LLM generates the transformation instead of selecting from deterministic ops, and failure leads to regeneration, not fail-closed no-op. Earlier analog: LLM-Vectorizer (2406.04693, Alive2-gated).

all_papers.title: MemTX: Transactional Belief Commit for Stateful Agent Memory
all_papers.authors: Xiaoyang Li, Yiqi Wang, Haohui Lu et al.
all_papers.what_it_does: Treats agent memory writes as transactions: snapshot isolation, a validate-and-commit pipeline, and cascading repair when committed beliefs are retracted.
all_papers.overlap_note: Transactional commit over persistent agent state. Its point that a bad commit propagates downstream echoes C3's finding that a single corrupted request changes later answers in 13/24 runs. Different domain and no formal equivalence.

all_papers.title: PatchOptic for Shared-State LLM Workflows with Projected Views and Verified Structured Updates
all_papers.authors: Zhaoyu Bai, Jiaqi Cai
all_papers.what_it_does: LLM steps see projected views of shared structured state and emit structured patches limited to declared write regions. Runtime verification blocks contract violations before commit.
all_papers.overlap_note: Verified structured updates committed to shared state, a generic analog of C1's guarded commit.

all_papers.title: Progent: Securing AI Agents with Privilege Control
all_papers.authors: Tianneng Shi, Jingxuan He, Zhun Wang et al.
all_papers.what_it_does: Symbolic privilege policies on tool calls are enforced deterministically before execution. An SMT solver ensures that policy updates can only shrink the action space without approval.
all_papers.overlap_note: Representative of the agent-security cluster of deterministic pre-execution tool-call gating. Related cluster: AgentSpec (2503.18666, ICSE 2026), ShieldAgent (2503.22738), Agent-C (2512.23738, SMT temporal constraints), CaMeL (2503.18813). These check security policy, not functional correctness.
all_papers.verified_by: abs page fetched (AgentSpec, ShieldAgent, Agent-C, CaMeL abs pages also fetched)

all_papers.title: Benchmarking LLM-Driven Network Configuration Repair (Cornetto)
all_papers.authors: Ioannis Protogeros, Rufat Asadli, Benjamin Hoffman et al.
all_papers.what_it_does: A benchmark of 231 network misconfiguration repairs (20-754 nodes) evaluated by formal verification against ground-truth specs. LLMs often introduce regressions, and the authors conclude that reliable automation needs formal-verification-guided workflows.

verdict.what_it_actually_does: Read from the README and the code (router.py, cli.py, llm/client.py, llm/tools_schema.py, constraints.py, abc_bridge.py, abc_synth.py). The full private system is a regex router of about 120 patterns over 95-98 handlers that answers most requests with no LLM call. The public build replaces that router with a stub, so every request goes to the LLM fallback. That fallback is a multi-turn ReAct-style tool-calling loop over 65 typed tool schemas: up to 8 rounds, several calls per round, tool errors returned to the model as JSON, and the model writes the final plain-text answer itself. The system prompt says it is "the fallback natural-language interpreter ... invoked only when a request did not match any of its patterns". ABC-backed depth and gate-count resynthesis runs on a deepcopy and is accepted only if `verify_equivalence` (ABC cec) proves it equivalent. The equivalence check cuts at registers: each DFF Q becomes a free input `__dff_Q__<inst>`, and D/RN/SN/CK become outputs `__dff_<PIN>__<inst>`. A fanout-cap bound set by one request is stored per design, re-checked after later requests and repaired by inserting buffers; a max-depth bound can only be reported. The README claims 0 crashes, every line answered, and all outputs equivalent on an offline replay of alpha (459 lines) and beta (680 lines). It says the regex router recognized 672/680 beta lines and states plainly that no accuracy rate is claimed.
verdict.overlap_with_us:
C1, closed catalog and no generated code: strong overlap in spirit. Their LLM only calls 65 typed deterministic tools and never writes netlists or scripts. Their README slogan ("The model is there to decide which operation a sentence means. It never computes the answer.") is close to our title. Differences:
- In their full system the LLM is not the router; a regex dispatcher is, and the LLM is only a fallback.
- Their LLM is a multi-step agent that can chain arbitrary reads and mutations within one request and writes free-form reply text. We map each request to exactly one intent and produce the reply deterministically.

C1, deterministic execution: same.

C1, equivalence gate with rollback: partial overlap only.
- Accept-only-if-cec-equivalent on a copy exists, but only for the ABC resynthesis tools (do_optimize_*).
- In the released LLM path, the deterministic in-place edits (remap_to_basis, limit_fanout*, insert_buffer_per_load, balance_depth_to_sinks, dedup, dangling removal, constant simplification, inverter collapse, rename) change the live design with no per-mutation cec, snapshot or rollback.
- Their "all outputs equivalent" figure is an offline replay measurement, not a runtime commit gate.
- A `check_equivalence_to_snapshot` tool exists, but the LLM calls it only if it chooses to.
- So no complete-mediation fail-closed commit gate appears in the released code. The private router may do more; we cannot verify that.
- The register-cut cec (Q as pseudo-input; D/CK/RN/SN as pseudo-outputs) is essentially identical to ours. We must not present that detail as novel.

C1, persistent state and grounding: persistent state is the same. Tool arguments are resolved against the current mutated design, and errors go back to the model.
- They have no bounded one-corrective-retry policy and no safe no-op: the model may keep retrying for up to 8 rounds, and on exhaustion partial text is returned.
- Their structural bounds persist across requests (same reading of Q&A A63), but violations are repaired after the fact by inserting buffers rather than rejected with rollback.
- In the public code, recording and enforcing those bounds happens only in the private router.
- Their gate-basis check is a tool option, not a commit guard.

C1, Proposition and drift: there is no formal proposition or assumption set. There are two informal echoes of our drift idea:
- The README says that preserving function, not crashing and answering every line are "necessary conditions, not sufficient ones".
- A rerun-refusal mechanism (mutating tools refuse to repeat an op unless force=true) was motivated by code comments recording that 6 of 18 measured rows deleted 691 gates in answer to a pure question, which is an equivalent-but-unwanted edit.
They do not define drift and do not measure whether it carries into later requests.

C2, routing study: none. There is no paraphrase set, catalog-versus-name ablation, retrieval study, classifier baseline or model comparison. The only number is regex-router coverage (672/680), which counts recognized lines, not correct ones.

C3, fault injection: low overlap. Their scripts/mutation_check.py applies code mutations ("knives") to check that the test suite catches them. That is test adequacy, not injecting corrupted routing outputs to validate runtime guards or measure downstream propagation. They did find and fix rename bugs that broke snapshot-equivalence bookkeeping, a loose parallel to our guard-bypassing rename, but by a different method.
verdict.differentiation: Concurrently with our contest work, the open-source netlist-agent [X] (August 2026) also lets an LLM pick from typed tools over a deterministic engine and accepts ABC-resynthesized candidates only after cec, but there the LLM is a multi-turn fallback behind a regex router that chains tool calls and writes its own reply text, its rule-based edits change the live netlist without a per-commit equivalence gate or rollback, and it reports no routing-accuracy measurement. We instead make the LLM the sole router that emits exactly one validated intent per request, send every mutation through a fail-closed commit gate with a stated soundness proposition that separates functional equivalence from request conformance, and measure routing accuracy (C2) and fault propagation (C3) directly.
verdict.where_to_cite:
1. Related Work, in the paragraph on systems for the same contest, next to the concurrent "Beyond Equivalence" submission. Use the differentiation sentence above, and cite it as a software artifact (GitHub URL plus access date), which is safe under double-blind because it is a third party.
2. Wording elsewhere: avoid claiming to be the first to propose "LLM decides the operation, engine computes the answer" for this contest. Frame C1's novelty as the fail-closed formalization: one intent per request, complete mediation, a commit gate with rollback, the Proposition with A1-A4, and the drift separation.
3. Architecture section: one clause saying the register-cut cec (DFF Q as pseudo-input; D/CK/RN/SN as pseudo-outputs) is a standard construction that [X] uses too.
4. If space allows, a footnote: unlike [X]'s after-the-fact buffer repair of structural bounds, we reject and roll back a violating mutation.

verdict.what_it_actually_does:
Read from the cloned repo: README, docs/ARCHITECTURE.md, ARCHITECTURE_NOTES.md, RELATED_WORK_BORROW.md, results.md, all routing_robustness reports, and the source files agent.py, tools.py, entity_guard.py, funceq.py, abc_io.py and planner.py.

1. Routing. A deterministic regex router (router.py, about 2k lines) is the main interpreter. A 'strong' match is dispatched directly with no LLM call. A 'weak' match is arbitrated against the LLM using hand-written rules for mutating vs read-only and history follow-ups. Only when nothing matches is gpt-4o-mini / claude-haiku-4.5 asked to choose exactly one of 63 function-calling tool schemas (11 mutating). It sees a short state summary, never the netlist, and gets one informed retry when required arguments are missing.

2. Name checking and fallback. Net and gate arguments are checked against the current design (entity_guard.py). Invalid names are fixed from the request text or by one LLM repair call. If that fails, the system reports 'Unable to complete' without changing anything. A ToolError triggers one informed LLM retry with a different tool. A final fallback lets the LLM write a typed multi-step JSON plan over read-only primitives.

3. Transaction gate. Mutating tools run on a clone, then design_equivalent is checked: ABC cec on a combinational view (DFF Q as PI, D as PO; CK/RN/SN pins are not checked). The design rolls back only on a 'differ' verdict. An 'unknown' verdict commits with a warning (the docstring says so). If ABC is unavailable, inconclusive or cannot align the boundaries, it falls back to exhaustive simulation for 16 or fewer free bits, otherwise to random simulation. optimize and limit_fanout skip the generic gate and use their own internal CEC checkpoints. Yosys equiv_induct exists only in the offline QA harness, not in the production gate.

4. Evaluation. An independent analysis oracle (39,176 cross-checks), about 766 paraphrase fuzz rows in 4 batches (LLM-only routing around 64-92% depending on batch and model, used to find and fix router bugs), and an official result of 567/628 (gpt-4o-mini) and 562/628 (haiku). Their post-mortem documents 29 points lost when 'break the total down by gate type (... XNOR ...)' was routed by regex to XNOR decomposition. The change passed the equivalence gate and the netlist stayed correct, but the answer was wrong.
verdict.overlap_with_us:
C1, closed catalog and no free-form generation: strong overlap. They also have a fixed tool set (63 tools, function calling, typed JSON-schema arguments), the LLM never computes or writes netlists or code, and execution is deterministic. Differences: (a) the main interpreter is a hand-written regex router, and the LLM decides only unmatched or weak-match requests. 669 of 674 official answers were identical under both models, so the LLM almost never decided anything. In our system the LLM routes every request and there are no rules. (b) They add an LLM-written multi-step plan over read-only primitives. Ours is exactly one intent per request.

C1, checking names against the current state with one corrective retry: real overlap that the candidate report missed. entity_guard checks net and gate arguments against ctx.design (the current, already changed design), then repairs from the request text or with one LLM call. An unresolved name gives an 'Unable to complete' answer with no change, and a ToolError gets one informed retry. Close to our grounding, retry and safe no-op, though implemented with heuristics rather than as a stated contract.

C1, equivalence gate before commit: overlap in shape, but theirs does not reject an edit when verification is inconclusive. It uses the same snapshot → CEC → commit/rollback pattern with Q as pseudo-input and D as pseudo-output. Differences: (i) an 'unknown' verdict commits with a warning, and random simulation can stand in for a proof, while we reject anything without a completed proof; (ii) their miter does not include CK/RN/SN; (iii) there are no generic structural-bound or gate-basis checks in the gate; (iv) optimize and limit_fanout skip the generic gate. A rename that changes PI/PO bit sets makes abc_cec return None, and design_equivalent then returns 'unknown', which commits. That is the same class of guard bypass we found and fixed.

C1, proposition (A1-A4) and separating functional correctness from request conformance: no formal counterpart, but the core observation is there. Their XNOR misroute is described in prose as 'the answer was wrong; the circuit was not', which is an instance of our drift. They do not name it, do not study it, and do not show it persisting into later requests.

C2, routing study: partial thematic overlap only. They measure LLM-only tool choice on about 766 paraphrases with the same two models (roughly 80-83% in batch 2 before fixes). This is a debugging tool for the regex router. It has no comparison of catalog formats (bare names vs full descriptions), no BM25 or retrieval comparison (retrieval is only proposed as future work), no supervised-classifier baselines, and no error taxonomy. It does not anticipate C2's findings. Their 29-point regex collision is outside evidence that rule-first routing is brittle on hidden wording.

C3, validation: no fault injection and no measurement of how errors spread to later requests. Their validation is an independent oracle plus official-score forensics. One anecdote matches our drift finding.
verdict.differentiation: Concurrently, another team in the same contest released code [cada1043] that also limits the LLM to function calling over a fixed tool set, checks argument names against the current design, and wraps every edit in a snapshot–CEC–rollback transaction. In that system a hand-written regex router decides most requests, the LLM handles only wording the router misses, and an edit is committed when equivalence is inconclusive (falling back to simulation). We instead route every request through the LLM against a closed catalog, reject any edit without a completed register-cut proof and structural checks, state the guarantee under explicit assumptions, and separate it from request conformance. Their post-mortem, in which a read-only gate-count question was carried out as an equivalence-preserving XNOR rewrite, is an independently observed instance of the drift we describe.
verdict.where_to_cite:
1. Related Work, in a 'same-benchmark / concurrent contest systems' paragraph next to 'Beyond Equivalence': use the differentiation text. Cite it as a non-archival GitHub release (team ID and URL), third person, so double-blind is preserved.

2. C1 or Design section: one clause noting that other contest systems also gate edits with CEC, and stating our difference precisely: we reject inconclusive results, the miter includes control pins, and we add structural and basis checks. Otherwise a reviewer who knows the contest may say the gate is the standard contest solution.

3. Drift / C3 discussion: cite their documented XNOR misroute as outside confirmation that equivalent-but-unwanted edits happen in deployed systems.

4. Optionally, C2 motivation: the 29-point regex collision as evidence against rule-first routing. State it neutrally.

Do not compare scores head to head. Their 567/628 leaves out the 46 optimisation requests, which are ranked against other teams, so it is not on the same scale as our 671.366/674.

Not strictly required: under DAC rules a GitHub repo is not prior publication. Citing is recommended because the design overlap is substantial and the contest reviewers may know it.

verdict.what_it_actually_does: I read the full report, the slides, the README and the core source (agent.py, tools/registry.py, tools/transform.py, transform/base.py, analysis/cec.py, analysis/graph.py, transform/depthopt.py). The report says the LLM (claude-haiku-4-5, with a gpt-4o-mini adapter) is kept to "selecting and parameterizing operations" over 42 JSON-schema-typed tools in five families, run by a from-scratch deterministic Python engine with Berkeley ABC behind it. In practice agent.py is a standard multi-turn function-calling loop (MAX_TOOL_ITERS=8) that can make several tool calls per request, keeps the full chat history, and lets the LLM write the final answer in free text; the transcripts show requests answered from memory with no tool call (test20 R18, test40 R13/R17). Transforms deep-copy the netlist, apply the rewrite, and check the copy against the original with a structural-hashing PySAT miter. The miter shares PI and DFF.Q variables and compares POs and DFF.D only, with DFFs matched by instance name; if SAT times out it falls back to ABC cec, and a failed check is "silently reverted". The evaluation reports coverage of the 40 public cases (no scores), depth reductions on 3 cases (up to 39%), zero disagreements between the SAT checker and ABC over 40 BLIF round-trips, a latency split, and 90 unit tests.
verdict.overlap_with_us:
C1, closed catalog vs free-form generation: same idea. Both use a closed set of typed deterministic operations (42 tools vs our ~80 intents), and the LLM never edits the netlist or writes code. The difference is the LLM's role. Theirs runs an open loop of up to 8 iterations with several tool calls, and the LLM writes the answer and may reason from chat history. Ours maps each request to exactly one intent.

C1, deterministic execution: the same.

C1, equivalence gate before commit, with rollback: partly the same. They also mutate a copy, run a register-cut SAT miter and commit or revert. Four differences:
- Their cut compares PO and DFF.D only, so changes to CK/RN/SN go unchecked (analysis/cec.py equiv_netlists, _pseudo_inputs).
- The gate is not fail-closed. tools/transform.py sets `verify = len(STATE.netlist.gates) < 2000` for remap_gates, and optimize_cone_depth uses `verify=False`; only the ABC path is self-checked with cec, and the native balancer is trusted "by construction". The test40 transcript commits a 4331-gate remap with "preserved by construction", so the report's "every transformation runs under the same guard" is contradicted by its own code.
- There are no structural-bound or basis-compliance checks.
- There is no formal proposition or assumption set like our A1-A4.

C1, persistent state and live-state grounding: they keep one persistent mutated netlist (a STATE singleton), but names are never grounded. graph.resolve_to_net passes unknown names through, so for example fanin_cone on a misspelled net returns "0 gates" instead of an error. Transforms raise an error on a missing name and the LLM may retry inside its loop, but there is no explicit validate-retry-once-then-no-op policy.

C1, functional guarantee vs request conformance: missing. They claim "never non-equivalent" and have no concept of drift or of wrong-but-equivalent edits.

C2, routing accuracy study: missing. They have no paraphrase set, no accuracy numbers, no catalog/retrieval ablation and no classifier baselines.

C3, fault injection: missing, and they report no official contest score.

Net effect: the high-level C1 pattern (an LLM picks typed deterministic ops, each checked for equivalence and committed or reverted) appeared publicly first in this report, in the identical setting. Everything that makes our C1 distinctive, and all of C2 and C3, is absent.
verdict.differentiation: An earlier, non-peer-reviewed course report for the same contest problem [Han 2026, Zenodo] also exposes a deterministic netlist engine to an LLM through 42 typed tools and checks rewrites with a register-cut SAT miter (ABC fallback) before committing them. However, it uses an open multi-call tool loop in which the LLM writes the final answer, does not ground names against the current netlist, skips the equivalence check for large basis remaps and for depth optimization, and evaluates neither routing accuracy nor fault tolerance. In contrast, we restrict the LLM to choosing a single grounded intent, make the equivalence and structural/basis checks mandatory for every mutation (with DFF control pins in the cut), state the resulting guarantee and its assumptions separately from request conformance, and measure routing accuracy and fault propagation empirically.
verdict.where_to_cite: Cite it in Related Work, in the paragraph on systems for the same contest, next to "Beyond Equivalence". Also soften any Introduction or contribution sentence that implies we are the first to pair LLM routing over typed deterministic operations with an equivalence check before commit for this problem. Our novelty claim should rest on what the report lacks: the check is mandatory for every mutation (fail-closed), names are grounded against the live netlist with one retry and a safe no-op, DFF CK/RN/SN are included in the register cut, there is a formal proposition with assumptions A1-A4, the drift/conformance separation, and the C2/C3 studies. verdict.title: AutoEDA: Enabling EDA Flow Automation through Microservice-Based LLM Agents (the title is the same in arXiv v1, v2 and the TODAES version; the candidate's title "AutoEDA: LLM-Driven Electronic Design Automation" is wrong, and no arXiv paper has that title)

verdict.first_version_date: 2025-08-01 (v1). v2 followed on 2026-02-24 and the ACM TODAES version went online on 2026-08-20 (Crossref). This is clearly prior art, not concurrent work.
verdict.venue: arXiv cs.AI (v1 2025-08-01, v2 2026-02-24); ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems (TODAES), online 2026-08-20, DOI 10.1145/3842675. The v2 PDF carries an ACM conference template header ("July 26-29, 2026, Long Beach, CA") with a placeholder DOI.
verdict.what_it_actually_does:
I read the full text of v1 and v2 (arXiv HTML) and the TODAES abstract via Crossref. AutoEDA controls RTL-to-GDSII flows (Synopsys DC synthesis, then Innovus placement, CTS and routing) from natural language. It has three layers: client, MCP server and executor.

- **Client (v2, Sec 3.2):** a locally fine-tuned Qwen3-0.6B maps the query to a schema-driven JSON IR {tool, params}. The schema has typed fields (numbers with units, enums, booleans, lists), stage identifiers and cross-stage constraints. Schema compliance comes from grammar-constrained decoding plus rule-based post-processing. v1 used prompt engineering on a frozen model with no fine-tuning.
- **MCP server (Sec 3.3):** decomposes the IR into four stage tools and tracks dependencies between stages. It validates parameters by constraint satisfaction: invalid values are clipped (for example, density capped at 1.0), missing parameters are inferred, and conflicting ones are resolved automatically. It then renders fixed, version-adaptive Tcl templates.
- **Executor (Sec 3.4):** runs the scripts. On a tool failure, a built-in fixer reads the logs and applies "rule-based bounded repairs".
- **Benchmark:** 10k synthetic prompt-config pairs (100 in v1), built by sampling configurations from the parameter schema and having an LLM rewrite each one in several styles, followed by rule checks.
- **Evaluation:** CodeBLEU-Tcl and BLEU against ground-truth Tcl, token usage, and execution success. The "9.9x accuracy" is CodeBLEU against direct gpt-4o generation; the journal abstract says "9.9x higher CodeBLEU" explicitly. The 97% token reduction is against in-context learning. Execution success is 100% vs 37% for the ICL baseline, on 5 designs. A multi-turn test feeds the whole history back each turn. The journal abstract adds that it "does not claim closed-loop QoR optimization or industrial sign-off quality."
verdict.overlap_with_us:
**C1, routing half (real overlap, and it predates us):**
- AutoEDA already sets up the EDA-specific principle that the LLM emits typed parameters into a closed schema, never Tcl, and that deterministic templates do the execution. v1 even says the design keeps "complete determinism".
- So our paper must not present "the LLM never writes scripts or code in an EDA agent" as new. Our headline "Routing, Not Reasoning" framing needs this citation.

**Where the C1 designs differ:**
- **Granularity:** AutoEDA has 4 coarse stage-level flow tools with roughly 15-25 parameters each. Its problem is slot-filling and configuration extraction, and one request can span several stages. We have about 80 fine-grained analysis/edit/optimize operations and exactly one intent per request, so our problem is mostly choosing the operation.
- **Validation philosophy is the opposite of ours:** AutoEDA repairs and proceeds (clip, infer, auto-resolve, auto-fix failed runs). We reject and fall back to a safe no-op after one corrective retry. Calling AutoEDA "fail-open" is our own label, not theirs, so in the paper I would say "repair-oriented" instead. Silent clipping or inference of user parameters is itself the kind of equivalent-but-unrequested change we call drift, and AutoEDA does not discuss it.

**C1, verification half: no overlap.**
- No functional verification of results: no equivalence checking or LEC, no structural or basis checks, no snapshot/commit/rollback. "Correctness" means the script executes and matches the reference Tcl.
- No grounding of name-typed parameters against a live design state. Its "state management" is versioned directories across flow stages (v1).
- No persistent, mutating design that later requests must be grounded on. The multi-turn test only refines parameters while replaying history.
- No proposition or assumptions, and no separation of the functional guarantee from request conformance.

**C2: weak overlap.**
- No routing or intent-accuracy study: no ablation of bare names vs full catalog, no BM25 example retrieval, no supervised-classifier baselines, no error taxonomy.
- Its ICL baseline adds Tcl template examples to direct generation, which is a different question from ours.
- One methodological echo: building the benchmark by sampling from the schema and having an LLM paraphrase each item in several styles resembles how we built our paraphrase stress set, so we should acknowledge it.

**C3: no overlap.** No fault injection, no study of cross-request error propagation, no contest setting.

**Setting:** RTL-to-GDSII on commercial tools with a fine-tuned 0.6B model, vs our flat gate-level netlist transformation with frozen gpt-4o-mini / claude-haiku-4.5.

**Corrections to the candidate report:**
- The title is wrong (see title field).
- The typed-IR, validation and repair details are confirmed by the v2 full text itself, so the cada1043 notes are right on this point.
- "Accuracy" means CodeBLEU, not task or routing accuracy.
verdict.differentiation: AutoEDA [Lu et al., TODAES'26] likewise keeps the LLM away from Tcl: a fine-tuned client emits a schema-typed JSON IR for four stage-level flow tools, which an MCP server validates and renders through fixed templates. Its validator repairs rather than rejects (it clips or infers parameters and auto-fixes failed runs), and it is evaluated on script fidelity (CodeBLEU) and execution success, with no check of the resulting design. Our agent instead routes each request to one of ~80 fine-grained operations over a persistent, mutating netlist, grounds names in the current state, and commits only after a register-cut equivalence proof, which keeps this functional guarantee separate from request conformance.
verdict.where_to_cite:
1. **Related Work, "LLM agents for EDA flows / tool calling":** next to ChatEDA, ORFS-agent and the MCP hardware benchmark, as the closest prior work on "LLM emits typed parameters, deterministic backend executes" in EDA.
2. **Introduction or the C1 contribution statement:** soften any claim that confining the LLM to typed parameters is new in EDA. Say our novelty is the closed fine-grained operation catalog combined with live-state grounding, fail-closed equivalence-gated commit with rollback, and the guarantee-vs-conformance split.
3. **One clause in C2 (stress-set construction):** schema-driven LLM paraphrase generation follows AutoEDA's benchmark pipeline.
4. **Optionally, the drift discussion:** contrast with AutoEDA's silent clipping and inference of parameters.

AutoEDA is not in our citation list and our paper sources do not mention it (no hit for "AutoEDA" or 2508.01012 in /home/joey123230/ICCAD_A .tex/.bib files), so it needs to be added. It is a TODAES paper from the Duke/Yiran Chen group, so DAC reviewers are likely to know it.

items.title: Evaluating LLM-driven User-Intent Formalization for Verification-Aware Languages (Lahiri, FMCAD 2024)
items.reason: States that a mechanical check cannot establish that informal NL intent was formalized correctly; a good conceptual anchor for our functional-guarantee vs request-conformance (drift) split, at an FMCAD venue close to DAC.

items.title: Graph-Symbolic Policy Enforcement and Control (G-SPEC): A Neuro-Symbolic Framework for Safe Agentic AI in 5G Autonomous Networks
items.reason: LLM planning constrained by knowledge-graph and SHACL validation in 5G; it has policy validation, no equivalence proof and no closed operation catalog.

items.title: What do LLMs need to Synthesize Correct Router Configurations? (Verified Prompt Programming)
items.reason: GPT-4 writes router configs and verifiers give localized feedback; foundational generate-then-verify, and it is exactly the LLM-writes-the-artifact design we avoid.

items.title: In-Context Learning for Text Classification with Many Labels

items.title: TinyAgent: Function Calling at the Edge (EMNLP 2024 Demo)

items.title: Efficient and Scalable Estimation of Tool Representations in Vector Space (Tool2Vec)

items.title: Disambiguation-Centric Finetuning Makes Enterprise Tool-Calling LLMs More Realistic and Less Risky (DiaFORGE; ACL 2026 Findings)
items.reason: Identifies 'near-duplicate tools vying for the same user intent' as a main failure of prompted frontier models, which is exactly our residual-error finding, so cite it to frame C2(c) as consistent; it fixes this by fine-tuning, whereas we use frozen models and catalog disambiguation.

items.title: ToolScope: Enhancing LLM Agent Tool Use through Tool Merging and Context-Aware Filtering (ACL 2026 main)

items.title: Model Context Protocol (MCP) Tool Descriptions Are Smelly! Towards Improving AI Agent Efficiency with Augmented MCP Tool Descriptions

items.title: Learning to Rewrite Tool Descriptions for Reliable LLM-Agent Tool Use (Trace-Free+)
items.reason: Learned description rewriting improves robustness as catalogs grow to 150+ tools; tangential to our hand-written closed catalog.

items.title: From SQL Generation to Tool Selection: A Domain-Oriented Pattern for MCP Servers (Bogliolo)
items.reason: Concurrent cross-domain statement of our thesis: replace query-time SQL synthesis with selection among parameterized domain tools ('Model Demotion': intent classification lowers the model tier needed; 3B goes from 0.583 to 0.929), which closely parallels 'routing, not reasoning' with mini models, so cite it as concurrent support.

items.title: Semantic Routing Framework for Multi-Domain Telecom Intent-Based Networking
items.reason: Fine-tuned contrastive sentence encoders reach 99.0/94.6% on 5 routes/22 branches with a 1,100-intent codebook, beating a cloud LLM, which is a possible reviewer counterpoint to our 'supervised at or below 73.3%'; explain that our label space (~80 near-synonym intents) and paraphrase shift differ.

items.title: RTLRewriter: Methodologies for Large Models aided RTL Code Optimization (ICCAD 2024)
items.reason: The LLM rewrites RTL directly with a fast verification pipeline; prior art that keeps LLM circuit changes only if verified, but with no closed catalog, persistent multi-request state or guarantee.

items.title: SymRTLO: Enhancing RTL Code Optimization with LLMs and Neuron-Inspired Symbolic Reasoning (NeurIPS 2025)
items.reason: LLM RTL rewriting with rule RAG, AST templates and formal-equivalence plus test validation; the LLM generates code, and there is no transactional commit over a persistent state.

items.title: ASPEN: LLM-Guided E-Graph Rewriting for RTL Datapath Optimization (Zhang, Deng, Kuehn, Ho, Yu, Zhang, Ren; Cornell/NVIDIA/UMD, MLCAD 2025)
items.reason: An LLM agent proposes and selects e-graph rewrite rules, so equivalence is preserved by the rewrite system; a contrast between correct-by-construction rules and our post-hoc CEC gate, not NL-request driven.

items.title: FormalRTL: Verified RTL Synthesis at Scale
items.reason: Multi-agent spec-to-RTL generation with formal equivalence against software reference models; generation and repair, not gated edits of an existing netlist.

items.title: Circuit Transformer: A Transformer That Preserves Logical Equivalence (ICLR 2025)
items.reason: Equivalence-preserving decoding for generated circuits (by construction); a different mechanism for functional preservation, useful only in positioning.
